text.en: A traveller from the Western Ghats to Rajasthan sees dense evergreen forest give way to thorn bushes. The reason is rainfall.

The average annual rainfall of India is 100 to 118 cm, but it is highly uneven.
Heavy rainfall (above 200 cm): western coast, Assam, south Meghalaya, Tripura, Nagaland, Arunachal; low rainfall (below 100 cm): Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, west UP and the Deccan interior.
Natural vegetation is the plant community unaffected by humans; climate, soil and landforms control it.
Tropical evergreen forests grow where rain exceeds 200 cm, in the Western Ghats, Andaman-Nicobar and the northeast, with rubber, mahogany, ebony and bamboo.
Tropical deciduous forests, called monsoon forests, grow in 100-200 cm rainfall and shed leaves in spring; teak and sal are their key trees.
Tropical dry forests grow in 50 to 100 cm rainfall and are transitional, with banyan, babool and khair.
Desert and semi-desert (tropical thorn) vegetation grows where rain is below 50 cm; babul, kikar and wild palms are common.
Mountain forests change with altitude: oak and chestnut at 1200-2400 m, chir at 900-1800 m, and pine, fir, spruce and juniper above 2400 m.
Mangroves or tidal forests grow in deltas and estuaries; Sundarbans of the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta is the largest.

prompt.en: Why are deciduous forests called monsoon forests and why do they shed leaves?

requiredIdeas.en: They depend on the monsoon rainfall
They drop leaves in spring and early summer to save water

points.en: Evergreen above 200 cm, deciduous 100-200, dry 50-100, thorn below 50.
